Prevention: Use of clean, nematode-free planting material:
Before planting, inspect carefully each planting piece for dry rot symptoms by scraping away the skin.
Use hot water treatment to reduce or eliminate nematodes from tubers (water temperature of 50-55°C for up to 40 min).
Seed tubers showing symptoms of dry rot (cracking and flaking) should not be used for planting.
Coating the setts in wood ash may help to reduce nematode numbers.
Some crops should be avoided prior to planting yams or as yam intercrops, i.e. cowpea, sesame, green gram, pigeon pea, kenaf, okra, tomato and melon.
Preference should be given to maize, groundnut, chilli, Indian spinach or sorghum.
Add cow dung into the mound to reduce nematode populations (as do applications of
NPK fertilizer and phosphorus alone, but nitrogen alone increases populations).
Use legume cover crops as restorative fallows to reduce nematode populations ( Aeschynomene histrix , Puerariaphas eoloides , Mucuna puriens and
Keep weeds to a minimum, especially those that are hosts of yam nematode, e.g.
Treat tubers after harvesting to prevent storage losses.
Removal of crop debris reduces soil populations nematode.
Monitoring: The feeding of the nematodes produces cavities.
The cavities become darker as the rot progresses (normally less than 2 cm).
Externally, cracks appear in the skin, which becomes crinkly, and parts flake off revealing the dark rot beneath.
Rots continue in storage and can lead to complete decay of the tuber as other rot-causing organisms take over.
Extensive rots can develop without cracking and flaking of the skin, and are only seen when the skin is scraped away.
Sometimes external symptoms are not obvious on the tubers.
There are no above ground symptoms.
Direct Control: After harvest, all undersized and rotten tubers should be collected and buried deeply or burnt.
